notes:
Fundamental Principle of Counting

  • If one event can occur in $m$ ways and another (independent) event in $n$ ways, both together can occur in $m\times n$ ways (multiplication principle); either/or uses addition.

Factorial

  • $n! = n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots2\cdot1$; $0! = 1$; $n! = n\cdot(n-1)!$.

Permutations (order matters)

FormulaMeaning
$^nP_r = \dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$arrangements of $r$ from $n$ distinct objects
$^nP_n = n!$arrange all $n$ objects
Circular$(n-1)!$ (clockwise/anticlockwise distinct); $(n-1)!/2$ if not
Repetition allowed$n^r$ (each of $r$ places has $n$ choices)
Objects not all distinct$\dfrac{n!}{p!\,q!\,r!\cdots}$ ($p,q,r$ = repetition counts)

Combinations (order does not matter)

  • $^nC_r = \dfrac{n!}{r!(n-r)!} = \dfrac{^nP_r}{r!}$.
  • $^nC_r = {}^nC_{n-r}$; $^nC_0 = {}^nC_n = 1$; $^nC_1 = n$.
  • Pascal's rule: $^nC_r + {}^nC_{r-1} = {}^{n+1}C_r$.
  • If $^nC_x = {}^nC_y$ then $x=y$ or $x+y=n$.
  • Number of diagonals of an $n$-sided polygon: $^nC_2 - n$.

Key distinctions

  • Use permutation when arrangement/order matters (seating, ranks, words); use combination for selection/grouping (committees, teams).
  • Word problems with vowels/consonants together: treat the group as one unit, multiply by internal arrangements.

Exam tip

KCET typically asks 2–3 questions from this chapter, mixing direct formula application ($^nP_r$, $^nC_r$), word-arrangement problems (letters together/apart, distinct letters), and committee-selection problems. Always double check whether the problem needs permutation (arrangement) or combination (selection) before applying a formula.

questions.q: The value of $^6P_2$ is
questions.trick: $^nP_r = n(n-1)\cdots$ down to $r$ factors.

questions.q: The value of $^7C_3$ is
questions.trick: $^nC_r = \dfrac{^nP_r}{r!}$ — compute the permutation then divide.

questions.q: The number of ways to arrange the letters of the word 'MISSISSIPPI' is
questions.explanation: MISSISSIPPI has 11 letters: M(1), I(4), S(4), P(2). Arrangements $= \dfrac{11!}{4!4!2!}$.
questions.trick: Divide $n!$ by the factorial of each repeated letter's count.

questions.q: How many 3-digit numbers can be formed using digits $1,2,3,4,5$ without repetition?
questions.explanation: $^5P_3 = 5\times4\times3 = 60$.
questions.trick: No repetition, order matters $\Rightarrow$ use $^nP_r$.

questions.q: How many 3-digit numbers can be formed using digits $1,2,3,4,5$ if repetition is allowed?
questions.explanation: Each of 3 places has 5 choices independently: $5^3 = 125$.
questions.trick: Repetition allowed, order matters $\Rightarrow$ use $n^r$.

questions.q: The number of ways 5 people can be seated around a circular table is
questions.explanation: Circular permutations of $n$ distinct objects $= (n-1)! = 4! = 24$.
questions.trick: Circular arrangement of $n$ distinct people $= (n-1)!$.

questions.q: In how many ways can a committee of 3 be chosen from 5 men and 4 women (no restriction)?
questions.explanation: Total people $=9$; choose 3: $^9C_3 = \dfrac{9\times8\times7}{6} = 84$.
questions.trick: No restriction $\Rightarrow$ pool everyone together and use $^nC_r$.

questions.q: In how many ways can a committee of 3 men and 2 women be formed from 5 men and 4 women?
questions.explanation: Choose men and women independently and multiply: $^5C_3 \times {}^4C_2 = 10\times6 = 60$.
questions.trick: Split by group, choose each independently, then multiply.

questions.q: If $^nC_8 = {}^nC_6$, the value of $n$ is
questions.explanation: $^nC_r = {}^nC_{n-r}$ with $r\ne n-r$ implies $8+6=n \Rightarrow n=14$.
questions.trick: $^nC_r={}^nC_{n-r} \Rightarrow$ the two lower indices add to $n$.

questions.q: The number of diagonals of a hexagon (6 sides) is
questions.trick: Diagonals $= {}^nC_2 - n$ (all segments minus the sides).

questions.q: How many words (with or without meaning) can be formed using all letters of 'EQUATION' (all distinct, 8 letters), taken all at a time?
questions.explanation: All 8 letters are distinct; arranging all of them gives $8!$ words.
questions.trick: All letters distinct, arrange all $\Rightarrow$ just $n!$.

questions.q: How many ways can the letters of the word 'DELHI' be arranged so that the vowels (E, I) always come together?
questions.explanation: Treat EI as one block: 4 units (D,L,H,[EI]) arrange in $4!$ ways; internal arrangement of E,I in $2!$ ways: $4!\times2! = 24\times2=48$.
questions.trick: Glue the 'together' letters into one block, then arrange blocks $\times$ internal order.

questions.q: The value of $^{10}C_4 + {}^{10}C_5$ is
questions.trick: Pascal's rule: $^nC_{r-1}+{}^nC_r = {}^{n+1}C_r$.

questions.q: Number of ways to select 2 cards from a deck of 52 playing cards is
questions.trick: Selecting cards (order irrelevant) $\Rightarrow$ use $^nC_r$.

questions.q: How many 4-letter codes can be formed from the 26 English letters if repetition is not allowed?
questions.trick: No repetition, order matters $\Rightarrow ^nP_r$.

questions.q: The number of ways to arrange 3 boys and 3 girls in a row so that boys and girls alternate is
questions.explanation: Two alternating patterns (BGBGBG or GBGBGB), each allows $3!$ ways for boys and $3!$ for girls: $2\times3!\times3! = 2\times6\times6=72$.
questions.trick: Alternating pattern: 2 pattern choices $\times$ arrangements within each group.

questions.q: If $^nP_2 = 30$, the value of $n$ is
questions.explanation: $^nP_2 = n(n-1) = 30 \Rightarrow n^2-n-30=0 \Rightarrow (n-6)(n+5)=0 \Rightarrow n=6$ (rejecting negative).
questions.trick: $^nP_2=n(n-1)$; solve the resulting quadratic, reject the negative root.

questions.q: The number of ways to distribute 5 distinct books to 5 students, one each, is
questions.explanation: This is arranging 5 distinct books among 5 students: $5! = 120$.
questions.trick: Distributing $n$ distinct items to $n$ people, one each, is just $n!$.

questions.q: Out of 6 novels and 3 biographies, the number of ways to choose 4 novels and 1 biography is
questions.trick: Choose each category independently with $^nC_r$, then multiply.

questions.q: How many words can be formed from the letters of 'APPLE' (5 letters with P repeated twice)?
questions.explanation: Total arrangements $= \dfrac{5!}{2!} = \dfrac{120}{2} = 60$ (dividing by $2!$ for the repeated P).
questions.trick: Divide $n!$ by the factorial of the repeated letter's count.

questions.q: The value of $0! + 1!$ is
questions.explanation: By convention $0! = 1$ and $1! = 1$, so their sum is $2$.
questions.trick: $0!=1$ by convention; add the other factorial directly.

questions.q: Using $^nC_r = {}^nC_{n-r}$, the value of $^{12}C_9$ is
questions.trick: Use $^nC_r={}^nC_{n-r}$ to switch to the smaller, easier index.

questions.q: In how many ways can a captain and a vice-captain be chosen from 11 players?
questions.explanation: Order matters (different roles), so this is $^{11}P_2 = 11\times10 = 110$.
questions.trick: Distinct roles $\Rightarrow$ order matters $\Rightarrow$ use $^nP_r$.

questions.q: The number of diagonals of a polygon with $n$ sides is given by the formula
questions.explanation: Total line segments between $n$ vertices are $^nC_2 = \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$; removing the $n$ sides gives $\dfrac{n(n-3)}{2}$ diagonals.
questions.trick: Diagonals of an $n$-gon $= n(n-3)/2$.

questions.q: The number of ways to arrange the letters of the word 'MATHS' (all distinct) is
questions.explanation: 'MATHS' has 5 distinct letters, so it can be arranged in $5! = 120$ ways.
questions.trick: All letters distinct $\Rightarrow$ arrangements $=n!$.

questions.q: A person has 3 different fruits and wants to choose at least one of them. In how many ways can this be done?
questions.explanation: Each fruit can be chosen or not, giving $2^3=8$ subsets; excluding the case of choosing none gives $2^3-1=7$.
questions.trick: 'At least one' from $n$ items $=2^n-1$ (exclude choosing none).

questions.q: The number of triangles that can be formed by joining 6 points in a plane, no three of which are collinear, is
questions.explanation: A triangle needs 3 non-collinear points: $^6C_3 = 20$.
questions.trick: A triangle needs 3 points, order irrelevant $\Rightarrow ^nC_3$.

questions.q: The number of straight lines that can be formed by joining 6 points in a plane, no three of which are collinear, is
questions.explanation: A line needs 2 points: $^6C_2 = 15$.
questions.trick: A line needs 2 points, order irrelevant $\Rightarrow ^nC_2$.

questions.q: The value of $^8P_3$ is
questions.trick: $^nP_r = n(n-1)\cdots$ for $r$ terms; multiply straight down.

questions.q: In how many ways can 8 people be seated in a row if 4 particular people must always sit together?
questions.explanation: Treat the 4 people as one block: this gives 5 units to arrange in $5!$ ways, and the block internally in $4!$ ways: $5!\times4! = 120\times24 = 2880$.
questions.trick: Glue the 'together' group into one block: arrange blocks $\times$ internal order.

questions.q: In how many ways can 6 people be seated around a circular table if two particular persons must always sit together?
questions.explanation: Treat the pair as one unit, giving 5 units in a circle: $(5-1)! = 24$ arrangements, times $2!$ for the internal order of the pair: $24\times2=48$.
questions.trick: Circular table + pair together: treat pair as one unit, use $(n-1)!\times2!$.

questions.q: The number of distinct arrangements of the letters of the word 'STATISTICS' is
questions.explanation: 'STATISTICS' has 10 letters with S repeated 3 times, T repeated 3 times and I repeated 2 times: $\dfrac{10!}{3!\,3!\,2!} = \dfrac{3628800}{72} = 50400$.
questions.trick: Divide $n!$ by the factorial of each letter's repeat count.

questions.q: If a task can be completed by method 1 in $m$ ways or by method 2 in $n$ ways, and the two methods cannot be used together, the total number of ways to complete the task is
questions.explanation: This is the fundamental principle of addition (sum rule): the two sets of ways are mutually exclusive, so they add.
questions.trick: Mutually exclusive methods: add the ways ('or' rule).

questions.q: If a task consists of two independent steps that can be done in $m$ and $n$ ways respectively, the total number of ways to complete the task is
questions.explanation: This is the fundamental principle of multiplication (product rule): $m\times n$.
questions.trick: Independent steps: multiply the ways ('and' rule).

questions.q: The number of ways to select a team of 2 boys and 3 girls from 4 boys and 5 girls is
questions.trick: Choose each group independently with $^nC_r$, then multiply.

questions.q: The number of ways to choose a chairperson and a secretary (different posts) from 10 committee members is
questions.explanation: Since the two posts are distinct, order matters: $^{10}P_2 = 10\times9 = 90$.
questions.trick: Distinct posts $\Rightarrow$ order matters $\Rightarrow$ use $^nP_r$.

questions.q: How many 3-letter codes (repetition allowed) can be formed from the 26 English letters if the first letter must be a vowel?
questions.explanation: The first letter has 5 vowel choices; each of the remaining 2 letters has 26 choices: $5\times26\times26 = 3380$.
questions.trick: Fix the restricted position's choices first, then multiply by the free positions.

questions.q: In how many ways can 4 different books be arranged on a shelf so that 2 particular books are never together?
questions.explanation: Total arrangements $=4!=24$. Arrangements with the 2 particular books together (block): $3!\times2!=12$. Never together $= 24-12 = 12$.
questions.trick: Never together $=$ total arrangements $-$ (together as one block).

questions.q: From 6 men, a committee of 4 is to be formed such that a particular man is always included. The number of ways is
questions.explanation: With that man fixed in the committee, 3 more must be chosen from the remaining 5: $^5C_3 = 10$.
questions.trick: Fix the required member, then choose the rest from what's left with $^nC_r$.

questions.q: The number of ways to divide 6 distinct objects into two unlabelled groups of 3 each is
questions.explanation: Choosing 3 of the 6 for one group can be done in $^6C_3=20$ ways, but since the two groups are unlabelled, each division is counted twice: $20/2 = 10$.
questions.trick: Split into two labelled groups with $^nC_r$, then divide by $2!$ since groups are identical.
